Bayer Balances a Wider Loss Against a Brighter Outlook and a Chinese First
sum: Bayer closed the books on a mixed third quarter of 2026 this week, pairing a net loss of EUR 672 million with an operating performance that beat the prior-year period — a split verdict that has done little to settle the debate among the analysts who cover the stock.

Revenue for the quarter came in at EUR 10.053 billion, up 4.1% in nominal terms and 1.9% once currency and portfolio effects are stripped out. EBITDA before special items climbed 6.9% to EUR 1.615 billion. Adjusted earnings per share landed at EUR 0.31, while the bottom line swung to a group result of minus EUR 0.7 billion.

The sell-side has drawn sharply different conclusions from the same set of numbers. UBS on Wednesday lifted its price target to EUR 66 from EUR 62 and reiterated its buy rating, pointing to the pharmaceutical division and its growth runway as the reason for the upgrade.

Jefferies moved in the same direction but stopped well short of enthusiasm. The house raised its target to EUR 48.50 from EUR 46 on the previous day while keeping its rating at "Hold." According to media reports, the analysts assume Bayer will land at the lower end of its full-year guidance range. Jefferies also flagged the unresolved glyphosate settlement as a lingering overhang.
Shares slipped 0.7% in the session. Coverage of the Jefferies note cited possible drags on the stock but stopped short of pinning the decline on any single cause.

Management's own forecast leans toward the more constructive reading. Bayer lifted its full-year outlook for EBITDA before special items to a range of EUR 9.8 billion to EUR 10.3 billion. Free cash flow guidance was revised to between minus EUR 1.5 billion and minus EUR 0.5 billion — still negative for the year, but a narrower shortfall than previously projected.
The company also trimmed its expected net debt at year-end to EUR 28.0 billion to EUR 29.0 billion, giving the balance sheet a little more breathing room as the litigation calendar fills up.

sum: Goldman Sachs lifted its price target on Bayer to 66 euros from 63.50 on Wednesday, keeping its "Buy" rating intact, according to media reports. The move puts the US investment bank in lockstep with UBS, which had raised its own target to 66 euros from 62 a day earlier while maintaining the same recommendation. Neither broker tied its decision to any single trading session.

The stock closed Tuesday at €55.46, up 2.6%, with Reuters attributing the positive market reaction to the pharmaceutical division's performance and the upgraded full-year outlook rather than to analyst activity. Shares added a further 2.5% today.

Bayer's third-quarter 2026 results, released Tuesday, showed group revenue of €10.053 billion, a nominal increase of 4.1%. Stripping out currency and portfolio effects, sales grew 1.9%. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, adjusted for special items, rose 6.9% to €1.615 billion.

The pharmaceutical unit did the heavy lifting. Its revenue climbed 8.0% to €4.680 billion, roughly 5% ahead of the Vara Research consensus cited by Reuters, while divisional EBITDA before special items jumped 23.6%. Management also nudged up its outlook for the division's adjusted EBITDA margin, now guiding to a 25% to 27% range for 2026.

That showing underpinned a brighter group forecast. Bayer now expects full-year EBITDA before special items of €9.8 billion to €10.3 billion at constant currencies, up from the €9.6 billion to €10.1 billion previously flagged.
The bottom line remains under water, though the damage is narrowing. Bayer booked a net loss of €672 million for the quarter, an improvement on the €963 million shortfall recorded a year earlier.

Attention now shifts to Missouri, where the proposed $7.25 billion Roundup settlement was still under court review. CEO Bill Anderson said Tuesday he anticipated a judicial ruling before Christmas, Reuters reported.

sum: Bayer raised several 2026 targets after reporting stronger third-quarter operating performance on November 3, with Pharmaceuticals driving the improvement. The company said the division is entering a new growth cycle, while Crop Science and Consumer Health continue to face market pressures.

According to Bayer's November 3 release, group sales rose 4.1 percent year over year to 10.053 billion euros. Adjusted for currency and portfolio effects, sales increased 1.9 percent. EBITDA before special items advanced 6.9 percent to 1.615 billion euros, including a positive currency effect of 36 million euros.

Pharmaceuticals was the central growth engine. Reported division sales increased 8.0 percent to 4.680 billion euros and rose 6.4 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis. EBITDA before special items climbed 23.6 percent to 1.292 billion euros, lifting the division margin by 3.5 percentage points to 27.6 percent.

Nubeqa and Kerendia led the advance, with currency- and portfolio-adjusted sales growth of 58.3 percent and 64.9 percent, respectively. Bayer said Nubeqa generated approximately one billion euros in quarterly sales, while Kerendia exceeded one billion euros over the 12 months ended September 30, 2026. Xarelto and Eylea continued to decline because of patent expiries, although Bayer said the pace of decline was slowing.

The other divisions were less supportive. Crop Science sales fell 2.4 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis, while its adjusted EBITDA dropped 41.3 percent to 101 million euros in the seasonally small quarter. Consumer Health sales were broadly stable on the same basis, but adjusted EBITDA declined 4.4 percent to 347 million euros.

Bayer raised its Pharmaceuticals adjusted EBITDA margin target to 25 to 27 percent from 23 to 25 percent previously. Group EBITDA before special items is now expected at 9.8 to 10.3 billion euros on a currency-adjusted basis, compared with the former range of 9.6 to 10.1 billion euros.

The company also lifted its free cash flow target by one billion euros to negative 1.5 to negative 0.5 billion euros and lowered its expected year-end net financial debt range to 28.0 to 29.0 billion euros from 29.0 to 30.0 billion euros.

Bayer shares surge in Frankfurt following its quarterly results and the upward revision of its 2026 forecasts
sum: In the third quarter, the group benefited from the recovery of its pharmaceuticals division, thanks to strong demand for its key medicines, which offset market pressures on the agricultural division and the Consumer Health segment

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - Bayer is soaring on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, buoyed by an upward revision to its full-year profit forecasts, following better-than-expected quarterly results, albeit still in the red. Since the start of the year, the share price has risen by over 42 per cent. In the third quarter, the Bayer Group benefited from the recovery of its pharmaceuticals division, thanks to strong demand for its key medicines, which offset market pressures on the agricultural division and the Consumer Health segment. Overall, the group recorded turnover of €10.05 billion for the quarter, up 4.1 per cent year-on-year, exceeding analysts’ expectations of €9.93 billion.

Sales in the Pharmaceuticals sector (prescription medicines) rose by 8 per cent to €4.7 billion on a reported basis. Growth was driven by the oncology drug Nubeqa and Kerendia, for the treatment of chronic kidney disease and heart failure, with sales up by 58.3 per cent and 64.9 per cent respectively (excluding currency and portfolio effects). “Thanks to these results, sales of Nubeqa reached around one billion euros in the third quarter alone, whilst Kerendia achieved blockbuster status by exceeding the one-billion-euro threshold in the 12 months from 1 October 2025,” the company states. The quarterly net loss narrowed to 672 million euros from a loss of 963 million euros last year and was affected by write-downs and legal costs. Excluding non-recurring items, EBITDA rose by 6.9 per cent to 1.6 billion euros.

Bayer Faces a Split-Screen Quarter: Slashed Profit Forecasts on One Side, a Courtroom Breakthrough o
sum: Bayer investors are heading into the November 3 third-quarter report with a paradox on their hands. The earnings bar has been lowered sharply over the past month, yet the company's legal overhang just produced its first genuinely encouraging courtroom signal since the US Supreme Court weighed in this summer.

Consensus now looks for earnings per share of €0.42 on revenue of €10.00 billion when the quarterly statement lands at 07:30 CET, ahead of the opening bell. The investor video call follows at 14:00 CET. What makes the setup unusual is the divergence inside those numbers: revenue estimates have barely budged, while EPS forecasts have been cut by 28.14% over the past 30 days. A stable top line, in other words, has not carried through to the bottom line.

Richard Vosser at JPMorgan reaffirmed an "Overweight" rating and a €61 price target on Friday, framing the defense verdict in Missouri as one more step toward containing the litigation. Jefferies took a cooler view the same day. Michael Leuchten kept a "Hold" and a €46 target, calling the first glyphosate trial win since the Supreme Court's June ruling encouraging but pointing to the same missing piece both analysts flagged: the judge has yet to sign off on the proposed settlement.

The verdict itself came in the case of Theresa Aretino et al., where a Missouri jury ruled unanimously for Monsanto, according to Bayer. Three plaintiffs had pursued claims of alleged product defects, misrepresentation and negligence. It marked the first glyphosate trial since the June Supreme Court decision, and dpa-AFX identified it as the concrete trigger for the share price move that followed. The stock was giving back 0.5% today.

Roughly 65,000 US Roundup claims remain outstanding. The proposed collective settlement provides for up to $7.25 billion spread over a maximum of 21 years. Final judicial approval is pending, which means that payment envelope cannot be treated as a resolved liability — and even a settlement drawn over two decades would not remove the importance of the operating business to Bayer's financial room to maneuver.
That matters because of the balance sheet. Net financial debt stood at €33.35 billion as of June 30, with the ratio of net debt to EBITDA at 3.2 times.

Bayer's Prostate Data and China Approval Lift the Stock, but JPMorgan's 61-Euro Target Is Still a Be
sum: Bayer shares climbed 3.2% on Monday, powered by two developments that arrived within days of each other: a closely watched prostate cancer readout and a Chinese regulatory green light. JPMorgan added its voice the same day, reaffirming an "Overweight" rating and a EUR 61 price target. Analyst Richard Vosser took a positive view of the DASL-HiCaP interim results. That endorsement supports the optimistic case — but it is an analyst's assessment, not evidence of business figures already booked.

Bayer released the Phase III data on Saturday. Darolutamid, marketed as Nubeqa, cut the combined risk of metastases or death by 58% versus placebo when added to hormone therapy and radiotherapy. The four-year metastasis-free survival rate came in at 95%, against 88% in the placebo arm. The trial enrolled prostate cancer patients at high risk of recurrence who were also receiving androgen deprivation therapy and radiation.

Two caveats belong alongside those numbers. The findings stem from an interim analysis, not the final readout of the study. And the 58% figure applies to the combined endpoint of metastases or death in the specific treatment setting studied — it cannot be extrapolated wholesale to other patient groups. The result describes a clinical benefit, not a revenue increase or an improvement in earnings.
A completed approval, a clinical signal, and a subgroup analysis

The three pieces of news carry different weight, and investors would do well to keep them apart. Asundexian's Chinese approval is a finished regulatory step: on Monday the NMPA cleared the drug under the brand name Sunharbo via an accelerated pathway, for adults after a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA, to reduce stroke risk. Bayer called it the first factor XIa inhibitor available in China. That approval covers one specific market and one specific indication — it says nothing about filings elsewhere.

Finerenon offers a third data point of a different kind. On October 22, Bayer presented subgroup analyses from the Phase III FIND-CKD trial at ASN Kidney Week 2026, covering chronic kidney disease patients without diabetes. Consistent effects on proteinuria and kidney function decline were reported versus placebo.

items.t: Bayer's Lab Wins Are Piling Up, but the Scoreboard That Counts Comes on November 3
Bayer's Clinical Wins Land, but the Earnings Test Is Set for November 3
sum: Bayer shares closed Wednesday at €45.65, up 3.9%, as investors digested a pair of pharmaceutical announcements that arrived from two very different stages of the drug-development pipeline. One is a regulatory green light in China. The other is an interim readout from a late-stage prostate cancer trial. Both strengthen the medical case for the company. Neither, on its own, tells shareholders anything concrete about revenue or profit.
That gap between clinical evidence and commercial results is where the real debate now sits.

The interim results, released Saturday, come from the Phase III DASL-HiCaP study. According to Bayer, NUBEQA — whose active ingredient is darolutamide — cut the risk of metastases or death by 58% versus placebo. The median follow-up period was 3.8 years. Both arms of the trial paired the treatment with ADT and radiotherapy; the only difference was whether patients received NUBEQA or a placebo alongside that standard backbone.

The four-year metastasis-free survival rate came in at 95% for the NUBEQA arm against 88% for the comparison group. Bayer thus reported both a relative risk reduction and absolute survival rates at a fixed observation point — a more complete picture than a single headline number.

What the trial does not supply is any estimate of sales or earnings. A clinical endpoint of this kind establishes efficacy within the studied regimen. Translating that into a revenue line requires assumptions about uptake, pricing and reimbursement that the data themselves cannot settle.

Separately, China's regulator approved Asundexian under the brand name Sunharbo. The indication covers adults who have suffered a non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk TIA, with the drug intended to lower the risk of further strokes. Bayer describes Asundexian as the world's first approved FXIa inhibitor — a genuine first-in-class milestone.

The two announcements should not be lumped together as equivalent wins. One is an interim analysis; the other is a granted marketing authorization in a specific territory for a specific patient population. They carry different evidentiary weight and different commercial timelines.

items.t: Bayer's Missouri Courtroom Test Looms Over a Year of Quiet Portfolio Surgery
sum: A fresh Roundup trial got underway this week in Missouri, and the timing could hardly be more delicate for Bayer. Three plaintiffs are taking on Monsanto, the group's US subsidiary, over allegations that the weedkiller was not adequately tested before it reached the market. Because the case is widely viewed as a bellwether for the glyphosate litigation still stacked up behind it, traders are watching closely — and they wasted little time reacting. Bayer shares shed 3.3% on the day the proceedings opened, closing at EUR 49.07.

The company rejects the claims. Its position is that glyphosate-based products are safe, and it has said it will keep cooperating with regulators as they revisit the science. That review is already moving: the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services have agreed to broaden their joint work on the ongoing glyphosate assessment.

What makes the Missouri hearing so consequential is that a proposed global settlement is already on the table. It would commit Bayer to payments of as much as USD 7.25 billion spread across 21 years. A hearing on that package was held roughly two weeks ago. If the judge declines to sign off, or sends it back for revisions, the company faces the prospect of years of individual trials with damage awards that are impossible to forecast.

That uncertainty remains the single biggest overhang for investors. Yet the equity has hardly behaved like a stock in distress. Since the start of the year it has gained 33%, and it currently trades at EUR 49.19. The 50-day moving average sits at EUR 48.61 — a level bulls would like to see hold.

While the courtroom drama plays out, management has been busy reshaping the balance sheet. On 21 September, Bayer agreed to sell the cancer drug Stivarga to Grünenthal in a deal worth up to EUR 375 million. Completion is targeted for late 2026 or early 2027. The logic is straightforward: free up cash, sharpen the pipeline's focus, and chip away at the debt pile left behind by the Monsanto acquisition.

Smaller disposals of this kind help at the margin, though they do not fundamentally alter the scale of the obligations. Investors are left weighing how quickly leverage can come down without starving the pharmaceutical business of the research spending it needs.

items.t: Bayer shares soar in Frankfurt; analysts are optimistic following the landmark ruling by the US Supreme Court
sum: Deutsche Bank has upgraded its recommendation to “buy”, following the ruling in the company’s favour in the billion-dollar glyphosate lawsuits relating to the herbicide’s alleged carcinogenicity

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - Bayer is leading the way on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, thanks to positive comments from Deutsche Bank analysts and also to the decision to set up a separate entity dedicated to the US operations of the controversial herbicide glyphosate. Shares in the German pharmaceutical and agrochemical giant rose by around 5 per cent, putting it in first place among the components of the DAX index. The share price climbed to €51.80, its highest level since August 2023.

Analysts at Deutsche Bank have upgraded their recommendation on the share to ‘buy’ from ‘hold’ and raised the target price from 45 to 60 euros, following the landmark ruling by the US Supreme Court in favour of Bayer concerning the multi-billion-euro glyphosate lawsuits relating to the herbicide’s alleged carcinogenicity.

DB’s experts believe that the group is now on a positive trajectory and that the focus should gradually shift to the fundamentals and growth prospects of the Crop and Pharma sectors. The German group has also announced its intention to consolidate its US herbicide-related activities into a dedicated subsidiary.

The spin-off forms part of the five-year programme to streamline operations presented last year for the Crop Science agricultural division, Bayer explained. The new company is called Ruveon and includes the production of Roundup, the brand name under which the glyphosate-based herbicide is marketed. Based in St Louis, Missouri, Ruveon will supply the US agricultural sector with “essential glyphosate-based products, meeting the highest standards of quality and service”, according to a press release. Ruveon remains a subsidiary of the Bayer Group.

The US Supreme Court has ruled in favour of Bayer regarding allegations of ‘failure to provide information’ concerning the labelling of glyphosate, which form the basis of the majority of the litigation. Although this ruling does not eliminate all legal risks, industry observers believe it will significantly reduce out-of-court settlements relating to Roundup cases.

Bayer AG has agreed to acquire up to 53,54,030 equity shares from Bayer CropScience AG, representing 11.91% of the paid-up equity share capital of Bayer CropScience Limited . The inter-se transfer between two promoters will be executed through the block deal mechanism on or after July 8, 2026. The transaction is exempt from the requirement to make an open offer under Regulation 10(1)(a)(ii) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011.

The acquisition price will not exceed the limits provided in the proviso to Regulation 10(1)(a) of the Takeover Regulations. The volume weighted average market price for the 60 trading days preceding the notice was INR 4,434 per share. Bayer AG confirmed that the acquisition price would not be higher by more than 25% of this computed price.

Following the transaction, Bayer AG's shareholding will increase from 8.43% to 20.34%. Bayer CropScience AG will cease to hold shares in the target company, reducing its stake from 11.91% to 0%. The total promoter group shareholding, including Persons Acting in Concert (PACs), remains at 71.43%.

Bayer AG and Bayer CropScience AG have confirmed compliance with applicable disclosure requirements in Chapter V of the Takeover Regulations. The acquirer declared that all conditions specified under Regulation 10(1)(a)(ii) regarding the exemption have been duly complied with. The disclosures were signed by authorized signatories Markus Goblet and Dr. Sven Vorstius on July 1, 2026.

Bayer’s Supreme Court Win in Roundup Case No ‘Silver Bullet’
sum: After years of legal setbacks that have cost billions of dollars over its top-selling Roundup weedkiller, Bayer AG finally got a resounding win in the biggest tribunal of all.

The US Supreme Court threw out a jury verdict won by a Missouri man who blamed Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Backing Bayer’s appeal, the court said Thursday consumers can’t sue Bayer for the absence of a cancer warning on its label, given that federal regulators concluded a cautionary statement wasn’t necessary.

Bayer’s shares closed up nearly 19% Thursday, the most since 2003, as investors hailed a decision that could stem the tide of big-dollar verdicts, even if it doesn’t completely solve the company’s Roundup problem. They were down as much as 1.9% in early trading in Frankfurt on Friday.

“Finally common sense has prevailed as regulators, who are in tune with the technical and scientific issues, are in a better position to determine what is safe than juries,” said David Herro, a portfolio manager at Harris Associates, which is one of Bayer’s five biggest shareholders.

Litigation over Roundup had wiped out more than $60 billion in market value since Bayer inherited the world’s most widely-used weedkiller through its purchase of agrochemical producer Monsanto in 2018. Once an icon of German industry, Bayer has struggled to get a grip on the crisis through successive management regimes.

Problems with Bayer’s crop-science division have also weighed on the company’s ability to boost the performance of its other units, including the pharmaceutical business. Current Chief Executive Officer Bill Anderson’s turnaround plan has focused on resolving the conglomerate’s legal woes while also cutting bureaucracy.

The stakes are also high for Anderson personally. The American took the helm of Bayer in mid-2023, tasked with bringing a close to the protracted litigation that’s already cost the company more than $10 billion. He has vowed to largely contain the situation by the end of 2026. Shareholders made clear that his ability to succeed will weigh heavily on how they judge his future at the company.
